summary: An announcement that the weather demonstration built for the ICCC show is generally available. It consists of two programs, a natural language program in LISP and a primitive Datacomputer, which talk over the network to answer English questions about weather.

eli5.summary: Two programs on two computers talk to each other to answer questions like did it rain in Boston, showing how networks can share work.

questions: how does the weather system work
subtitle: A networked natural language system for answering weather questions

tldr.problem: Answering questions about weather data requires both natural language understanding and access to large data stores, which are difficult to run on a single machine.
tldr.mechanism: The system splits into two programs on two hosts: a LISP program that understands English sentences and a Datacomputer that stores and retrieves weather data, communicating over the network using Datalanguage.
tldr.outcome: Users could ask questions like 'Did it rain in Boston on October 7?' and get answers by having the natural language system query the datacomputer across the network.

facts.label: Data pages
facts.value: About 2,400 pages of real data plus 200 for inversion

today: This was a demonstration of early network-based distributed computing, where tasks were split across multiple hosts. Natural language processing was still a novel and difficult task in 1973, and the limited capabilities documented here reflect the state of the art at the time.

sections.title: The Weather Demo System
sections.content: This announcement describes a demonstration system called Weather that was originally built for the ICCC show and is now generally available. The system consists of two independent programs that work together over the network to answer English-language questions about weather data, such as 'Did it rain in Boston on October 7?'
sections.eli5: A demo that answers weather questions by having two programs on different computers ask each other for information.

sections.title: Two-Part Design
sections.content:
The natural language half is written in LISP and is a modification of a system developed by T. Winograd at MIT. It parses English sentences and figures out what information is being requested. The datacomputer half is a primitive database system that stores weather observations and can search them based on requests from the natural language program. The two programs communicate using Datalanguage, a query language sent over the network.

The weather data contains information from October, about 4,000 cities, and includes observations such as temperature, precipitation, wind speed and direction, visibility, cloud cover, and general conditions.
sections.eli5: One program understands English questions, the other stores data. They send messages back and forth over the network to find answers.

sections.title: Using the System
sections.content:
After starting the Weather program, the system prompts for a Julian date (the day number of the year). To get the best results, the user would enter 300, which corresponds to October 26. The system then prompts with 'READY' and accepts English sentences about weather, such as 'What was the temperature in Boston yesterday?' or 'Has it rained in Boston recently?'

If the system cannot understand a request, it returns a default message. The system does not understand complex requests like questions with conjunctions or negations, and it does not know about snow. Users can end a session by typing 'GOODBYE.' The average response time is about one minute.
sections.eli5: You type a question, and the program tries to understand it and find the answer in the weather database.

sections.title: Availability and Limitations
sections.content: The natural language LISP program requires significant CPU and memory resources. Running it on your own machine is preferred because it is a major load on the CCA system. If it must run on the CCA machine, checking with CCA staff beforehand is necessary. The datacomputer is less demanding and can run during non-prime time (outside 1 to 5 PM Eastern Time). Only one user at a time can use the datacomputer, a limitation that would eventually be lifted. Wednesday mornings are reserved for preventive maintenance when the machine will be down from 9 AM to noon or later.
sections.eli5: Running this takes a lot of computer power and time, so it works best when people are not too busy.
